extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (patent examining corps); patent practitioners may also use as guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on how to evaluate claims for subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A Prong One, Step 2A Prong Two, and Step 2B), including evidentiary support and required Office action language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to specific claim limitations and explain why they are considered an exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature). When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter the limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of abstract idea must mirror claim recitation and map to abstract idea groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, if not within those groupings, use the "tentative abstract idea" procedure and provide justification for treating a specific limitation as an abstract idea. While not required, the explanation may cite an appropriate court decision; avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match and ensure the cited decision is reasonably tied to the facts. Sample explanation: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the "mental process" grouping.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain laws of nature and natural phenomena as recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify the law/natural phenomenon as it is recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned rationale (see MPEP § 2106.04(b)). Sample explanations: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body...' or 'The claim recites X, which is a natural phenomenon because it occurs in nature and exists in principle apart from any human action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain product-of-nature exceptions (markedly different characteristics analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner finds a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and explain why there is no indication of marked differences in structure, function, or other properties. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(b)-(c). Sample: 'The claim recites X, which was isolated from naturally occurring Y. Because there is no indication that isolation resulted in a marked difference, X is a product of nature exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether they integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the integration inquiry by addressing the additional elements both individually and in combination, using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they are well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be eligible (Diamond v. Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do or do not add 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If certain claim elements are concluded to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the options specified in Subsection III. Address whether additional elements add meaningful limitations or merely implement the exception on generic computer components, add insignificant extra-solution activity, or merely impose a field-of-use limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections only when conclusion is readily apparent to examiner based on expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries that the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not amount to significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why the additional elements do integrate an exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 and MPEP § 2106.07(c) for clarifying the record when a claim is found eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support required when asserting elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' (evidentiary requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not assert that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more of the specified supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted supports (Subsection III): (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or an applicant statement demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional (e.g., described as commercially available or not described in detail because well-known); (B) citation to one or more relevant court decisions (ensure the claim limitations match in manner and generality); (C) citation to a publication (book, manual, review article) demonstrating wide prevalence or common use in the relevant field (single patent/publication usually insufficient); (D) an examiner taking official notice based on personal knowledge that an element is widely prevalent or in common use (use only when certain; see MPEP § 2144.03 for procedures). Do not base a finding solely on the specification being silent regarding the element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary burden rules at different steps of the analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts treat eligibility as a question of law, but factual issues may underlie Step 2B inquiries (e.g., whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Step 2A Prong One, a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception is sufficient and no evidence (publications, affidavits) is required. At Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, no evidence is required unless asserting that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional — in which case the examiner must provide one of the supports listed in Subsection III. Relevant case law (e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt., OIP Techs., DDR, Berkheimer) is cited for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of generic computer components and generic computing functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind courts have found some computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea when generic components in combination perform functions that are not merely generic (see DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for examples of generic computing functions found to be mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer. Explain why generic recitations amount to no meaningful limitation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations do not make claims eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use generally do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explanation why such limitations fail to integrate the exception into a practical application. Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process of computing area (mathematical relationship) does not add a meaningful limitation; limiting use to a particular industry (Parker v. Flook) is insufficient. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) and (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of claim element combinations — new combinations may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating additional elements, examiners must consider elements both individually and in combination, because a new combination of steps in a process may be patent eligible even though all the steps individually were well known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Diamond v. Diehr as authority. It is particularly critical to address the combination of additional elements because while individually-viewed elements may not integrate an exception, their combination may amount to significantly more by meaningfully limiting the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05 for Step 2B considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice — suggest claim elements from the specification that could make claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific specification disclosure that could be used to amend claims to add meaningful limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution — perform complete examination on other requirements despite §101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements: 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and 101 (utility, inventorship and double patenting) and non-statutory double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prescribed form paragraphs for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific form paragraphs for rejections involving statutory categories and judicial exceptions: 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, and when applicable 7.05.017 (tentative abstract idea requiring TC Director signature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph rules: 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections. 7.05 should precede 7.05.01 and be followed by a detailed explanation using one or more of the specific form paragraphs. For claims directed to a judicial exception without providing significantly more, use 7.05.016 (and 7.05.017 for tentative abstract ideas). See examiner notes for bracketed instructions on filling each form paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content for form paragraph 7.05.016 (bracketed instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.05.016 must state that the claimed invention is directed to [law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea/product of nature] without significantly more and include bracketed material that identifies the exception, how it is recited, why it is not integrated into a practical application, and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the examiner notes: bracket 1 — identify type of exception; bracket 2 — identify the exception by reference to how recited in the claim and explain why it is an exception (e.g., map to abstract idea grouping or explain product-of-nature comparison); bracket 3 — explain why combination of additional elements fails to integrate into a practical application (examples: generic computer elements merely implement abstract idea, data gathering is insignificant); bracket 4 — explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. For tentative abstract ideas, include 7.05.017 and TC Director signature.
